statutes.act: Read With Section 34 Of The Indian Penal Code

facts: One Kumari Rekha Sengar (PW-2), who is the complainant in the present case, got a phone call from her mother Smt. Shashi Prabha (now deceased) at about 11.00 to 11.30 pm on 02.09.2000 narrating that complainant's brother-in-law (Jeeja), namely, Suresh Pal Singh @ Guddu along with his friend had come to their house in Etawah, Uttar Pradesh, demanding Rs.50,000/- from her father and on refusal to meet the demand, they became very angry.
The complainant herself had a talk with her brother-in-law and tried to pacify him but she failed as he cut the telephone call.
Later when the complainant failed to have further communication on telephone, she left for her parents' house from Delhi.
On reaching her parents' house she saw dead bodies of her father, mother, two sisters and their pet dog.
Law was set into motion after an FIR was registered by the complainant on the basis of written report.
issues: Whether compelling an accused to provide his fingerprints or footprints etc. would come within the purview of Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India i.e. compelling an accused of an offence to be a 'witness' against himself?
petitioner_arguments: The case has been proved on the basis of circumstantial evidence.
PW-1 has proved the factum of both accused last seen together outside the main door of house of deceased.
Memo of recovered articles as a result of disclosure statement was not only admissible against accused Suresh Pal (now deceased) but is also admissible against accused-respondent herein.
Confessional statement of the co-accused who died pending trial is relevant against the accused-respondent also.
respondent_arguments: The recovery of bag and articles (Ext.1) cannot be made admissible against co-accused who is respondent herein.
Prosecution has not produced any witness or evidence to connect the accused-respondent with recovered bag or articles.
Complainant (PW-2) has also improved her statement apropos presence of the accused-respondent.
There was no mention of name or other details of the accused-respondent either in the written complaint/FIR or in the statement made before police.
court_reasoning: The taking of impressions or parts of the body of an accused person very often becomes necessary to help the investigation of a crime.

It is as much necessary to protect an accused person against being compelled to incriminate himself, as to arm the agents of law and the law courts with legitimate powers to bring offenders to justice.
holding: We are of the considered opinion that the following question would play a crucial role in helping us reaching an upright decision: Whether compelling an accused to provide his fingerprints or footprints etc. would come within the purview of Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India i.e. compelling an accused of an offence to be a 'witness' against himself?
